55: TBP recognises the TATA box (−33). Upstream, CREB (on the CRE) and SRF–ELK1 (on the SRE) await the signal: Ca²⁺ entering through NMDA receptors and calcium channels, or BDNF via TrkB and ERK.
56: TFIID (TBP on TATAAA), TFIIA, TFIIB, Pol II–TFIIF, TFIIE, TFIIH. CREB phosphorylated on Ser133 (CaMKIV, PKA, RSK/MSK) recruits CBP/p300; ELK1 phosphorylated by ERK activates the SRF complex on the SRE; enhancers e1–e5 move in and produce eRNAs.
57: On FOS this is the resting state: a polymerase waits here permanently, and the stimulus merely releases the pause — hence a response within minutes.
58: The FOS 3′UTR carries AUUUA motifs: the mRNA will be deadenylated then destroyed within about fifteen minutes.
60: You arrive with the blood in a bone marrow sinusoid. Hold ▲ while aiming at the ◎ marker: the ship shrinks by itself as it approaches, crosses the wall, then lands on the erythroblast's clathrin-coated pit, flagged by golden rings. Or tap “Take me to the entrance”.
61: You are now in the cytosol. Enlarge the ship (+) to go faster, avoid the organelles and head for a nuclear pore.
62: Binding to the TfR1 receptor: the ship passes itself off as a holo-transferrin.
63: Invagination: AP-2 and clathrin bend the membrane into a ≈100 nm pit.
64: Early endosome: the V-ATPase acidifies the lumen (pH ≈ 5.6). Fe³⁺ leaves transferrin, is reduced to Fe²⁺ by STEAP3 and exported to the cytosol by DMT1. Apo-transferrin and TfR1 are recycled to the surface.
66: You arrive with the blood in a liver sinusoid. Hold ▲ while aiming at the ◎ marker: the ship shrinks by itself as it approaches, slips through a fenestra of the endothelium, then lands on the hepatocyte's clathrin-coated pit, flagged by golden rings. Or tap “Take me to the entrance”.
67: You are now in the hepatocyte cytosol. Enlarge the ship (+) to go faster, avoid the organelles; the nucleus is at the centre.
68: Binding to the LDL receptor: the ship (20 nm) passes itself off as an LDL, whose apolipoprotein B-100 is recognised by the cysteine-rich repeats of the receptor.
69: Invagination: the adaptor ARH (LDLRAP1) reads the NPVY motif of the receptor tail and links it to AP-2 and clathrin, which bend the membrane into a ≈100 nm pit.
70: Early endosome: at pH ≈ 6 the receptor folds back and lets go of its LDL, then returns to the surface (≈ 10 min per round trip, hundreds of cycles) — unless PCSK9 escorts it and condemns it to the lysosome. The LDL will be digested there; NPC2 then NPC1 extract its cholesterol, which switches off SREBP-2: fewer receptors, less synthesis.
72: Between the hepatocyte and the sinusoidal capillary. The sinusoidal endothelium (dark slabs above you) is pierced by 100–150 nm fenestrae and has no basal lamina: plasma bathes the hepatocyte microvilli directly. The yellow spheres are LDL (≈ 22 nm, one apolipoprotein B-100, ≈ 1,500 cholesteryl esters). Stellate cells, the vitamin A store, live here; Kupffer cells patrol the sinusoid.
74: Bristling with microvilli that multiply the exchange surface with plasma. In: NTCP and OATP (bile acids, bilirubin, drugs), GLUT2 (glucose, both ways), receptors for LDL, insulin, glucagon, asialoglycoproteins. Out: albumin, clotting factors, VLDL, glucose, urea. A belt of tight junctions separates it from the canalicular pole.
76: Faces apposed to neighbouring hepatocytes, without microvilli: tight junctions (along the canaliculus), desmosomes and gap junctions — plaques of connexons (connexins 32 and 26), each channel linking two cytosols and passing ions and small molecules (< 1 kDa), which spreads calcium signals along the hepatocyte plate.
78: A ≈ 1 µm groove between neighbouring hepatocytes, lined with microvilli and sealed on each side by tight junctions (claudins, occludin; rows of pale beads). ABC pumps secrete bile into it against steep gradients: BSEP/ABCB11 (bile salts, green), MDR3/ABCB4 (phosphatidylcholine, orange), ABCG5/G8 (cholesterol), MRP2/ABCC2 (conjugated bilirubin, blue). Their deficiencies: familial cholestasis PFIC2 and PFIC3, Dubin-Johnson syndrome. A ring of actin and myosin under the membrane propels the bile.
80: An 839-amino-acid glycoprotein: seven cysteine-rich repeats that bind apoB-100 and apoE (Ca²⁺ required), an EGF-precursor homology domain with a β-propeller (ligand release at acidic pH), an O-glycosylated stalk, a cytosolic tail with an NPVY motif. The liver clears most of the body's LDL. Loss-of-function variants: familial hypercholesterolaemia. Land on the flagged pit (size ≤ 30 nm).
82: LDL receptors gather here thanks to the adaptor ARH (LDLRAP1), which links their NPVY motif to AP-2 and clathrin; its absence causes autosomal recessive hypercholesterolaemia. Clathrin triskelia assemble into a cage of pentagons and hexagons that bends the membrane.
84: A metabolic crossroads: glycolysis and gluconeogenesis, glycogen synthesis and breakdown (magenta rosettes), fatty acid synthesis, three of the five steps of the urea cycle, glutathione conjugation. The speciality depends on position in the lobule: periportal (gluconeogenesis, ureagenesis, β-oxidation) or pericentral (glycolysis, lipogenesis, cytochromes P450, glutamine synthetase). Hepatocytes are often polyploid, sometimes binucleate. Avoid the organelles!
86: Several 80S ribosomes (25–30 nm; 4 rRNAs and ≈ 80 proteins) translate the same mRNA at ≈ 5 amino acids per second. Free polysomes make the proteins of the cytosol, nucleus, mitochondria and peroxisomes — here mostly metabolic enzymes. Secreted proteins are translated on the ER.
87: A hepatocyte holds some 1,000 to 2,000 of them, ≈ 20 % of its volume (only some are drawn). Besides the respiratory chain and the Krebs cycle: fatty acid β-oxidation and, when fasting, ketogenesis (HMG-CoA synthase 2), the first two steps of the urea cycle (CPS1, OTC), pyruvate carboxylase (start of gluconeogenesis), 27-hydroxylation of cholesterol (CYP27A1, bile acid pathway). Circular mitochondrial DNA of 16,569 bp (yellow dots), maternally inherited.
89: Highly developed, in stacks of parallel cisternae: it makes the plasma proteins — albumin (≈ 10–15 g per day for the whole liver), fibrinogen, clotting factors, transferrin, apolipoproteins, hepcidin. ApoB-100 receives its first lipids here from MTP: the beginning of VLDL. Folding (BiP, calnexin), disulfide bonds, N-glycosylation, γ-carboxylation of the vitamin K-dependent factors.
91: Particularly abundant. Cytochromes P450 (CYP3A4, CYP2E1…) and their reductase: oxidation of drugs and toxins (phase I), inducible by phenobarbital or rifampicin; UDP-glucuronosyltransferases (phase II), including UGT1A1 which conjugates bilirubin; synthesis of cholesterol (HMG-CoA reductase, the statin target) and of bile acids (CYP7A1); glucose-6-phosphatase, which releases glucose to the blood.
93: Several stacks of polarised cisternae (cis → medial → trans). Maturation of plasma glycoproteins: without their terminal sialic acid they would be taken back up by the asialoglycoprotein receptor; maturation of VLDL (30–80 nm); sorting to the sinusoid, to the canaliculus (bile transporters) or to lysosomes (mannose-6-phosphate).
94: Several hundred per hepatocyte. β-oxidation of very-long-chain and branched fatty acids, last steps of bile acid synthesis (side-chain shortening, conjugation to glycine or taurine), plasmalogen synthesis, glyoxylate detoxification by AGT (deficient in primary hyperoxaluria type 1); catalase destroys H₂O₂ here. Proteins are imported already folded (PTS1 signal, PEX peroxins).
